The finding that some models converge more slowly than others, or more slowly than humans, is therefore a meaningful result, even if they would all converge eventually.\\n\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Individual Behavior}\\n\\\\label{sec:individual}\\nBefore turning to model-specific behavior, we briefly describe the typical dynamics of a single experiment run. From there, agents move in small increments undercutting or overbidding the previous quote, until the spread becomes small enough for an agent to cross it and execute a trade. This pattern repeats across iterations and rounds. We document key findings  below.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Incremental Order Improvement.}\\nThe vast majority of order improvements across our experiments are in small \\\\$0.01 increments. Agents thus face a profit-maximization vs. transaction-completion tradeoff, and our results suggest they heavily prioritize the former with little regard for the risk of failing to trade. \\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Heterogeneous Willingness to Cross the Spread.}\\nModels differ substantially in the bid-ask spread they tolerate before initiating a trade. This is a direct manifestation of the profit-vs-completion tradeoff, with the two models occupying different points on the frontier. Nothing stops them from placing a more aggressive offer that secures a reasonable rent; if it fails to trade or is undercut by rivals, they can simply revise it in a later iteration. Interestingly, in GPT Small this pattern is partly reversed: in some runs the first-moving side posts at its reservation price while the second-moving side attempts to extract rent (Figure \\\\ref{fig:first-mover}, right panel).\\n\\n\\n\\\\section{Analysis of Reasoning of LLM Traders}\\n\\\\label{sec:reasoning}\\nSection~\\\\ref{sec:individual} identified willingness to cross the spread as the\\nbehavioral lever separating functioning markets from stalled ones. Nonetheless, this is the condition in which the convergence pattern is most visible.\\n\\nIt is notable that the smaller, less capable model produces more efficient markets than any of the two larger ones. Nonetheless, we find this result surprising and counter-intuitive at first, and we return to it in Section \\\\ref{sec:discussion}. \\n%\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Aggressive Rent-Seeking Suppresses Trade Volume.}\\nThe number of trades in the GPT Large condition is substantially below other conditions and well below the equilibrium quantity of 6, averaging 2.2–3.8 trades per round. The result is depressed allocative efficiency: 0.36–0.67 across rounds, which is on average lower than in the case of the two other models. This is a clean illustration of how a single behavioral feature at the individual level (unwillingness to cross spreads) translates into large differences in market-wide outcomes. However, even if it were the case, the speed of convergence is itself a substantive outcome. The allocative efficiency of a double auction is fully realized only in equilibrium. A market that takes longer to get there is, for the whole of that path, less efficient and its price signal less trustworthy. The finding that some models converge more slowly than others, or more slowly than humans, is therefore a meaningful result, even if they would all converge eventually.\\n\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Individual Behavior}\\n\\\\label{sec:individual}\\nBefore turning to model-specific behavior, we briefly describe the typical dynamics of a single experiment run. The first agent to act posts an offer trying to secure some reasonable rent, with the exact value varying widely across runs. From there, agents move in small increments undercutting or overbidding the previous quote, until the spread becomes small enough for an agent to cross it and execute a trade. This pattern repeats across iterations and rounds. We document key findings  below.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Incremental Order Improvement.}\\nThe vast majority of order improvements across our experiments are in small \\\\$0.01 increments. Agents improve standing orders by the smallest possible amount, ensuring their offer becomes the new standing quote while preserving as much potential profit as possible. This behavior carries a cost: small improvements are more likely to be undercut by other agents, and the round may finish before the agent transacts. Agents thus face a profit-maximization vs. transaction-completion tradeoff, and our results suggest they heavily prioritize the former with little regard for the risk of failing to trade. \\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Heterogeneous Willingness to Cross the Spread.}\\nModels differ substantially in the bid-ask spread they tolerate before initiating a trade. Gemini Large agents cross spreads of approximately \\\\$0.50 on average, while GPT Large agents mostly wait until the spread approaches zero, with very few exceptions. This indicates that Gemini Large agents respond more readily to profitable trade opportunities and accept smaller per-trade profits, while GPT Large agents leave no potential profit on the table even when profitable trades are available. This is a direct manifestation of the profit-vs-completion tradeoff, with the two models occupying different points on the frontier. GPT Small agents are an intermediate case, with buyers crossing spreads of around \\\\$0.25 on average while sellers mostly waiting until the spread closes.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Role Asymmetries.}\\nIn GPT Small, we observe substantial behavioral differences between buyers and sellers. This asymmetry extends to trade initiation. While the absolute number of trades initiated by each side is broadly equal, the fill rate — the fraction of an agent\'s orders that result in a transaction — is markedly higher for buyers (see the supplementary material). The mechanism is that sellers submit roughly three times as many orders as buyers, but many of these orders are small incremental improvements. Buyers, by contrast, often refrain from posting, and when they do post, they make larger improvements that are more likely to result in a transaction. The pattern is partly reversed.}\\n\\\\label{fig:first-mover}\\n\\\\end{figure*}\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Opening-Offer Anchoring.}\\nThe first offer placed in an experiment serves as an anchor for subsequent agents. For agents on the same side as the opening offer, this is unsurprising because, to have their own offer accepted, they must improve on the standing quote, which mechanically ties their behavior to it. What is surprising is that agents on the opposing side react to the first offer as well, even though they have yet to post any offer of their own and are under no such constraint. Nothing stops them from placing a more aggressive offer that secures a reasonable rent; if it fails to trade or is undercut by rivals, they can simply revise it in a later iteration. Yet agents often do not pursue this strategy.\\n\\nThis produces a systematic asymmetry between the side that moves first and the opposing side. The distribution of opening offers for the first-moving side is wide, reflecting heterogeneous strategies for extracting rent in the absence of any reference point. The distribution of opening offers for the second-moving side is much tighter and anchored on the first offer.\\n\\nThis effect takes an extreme form in GPT Large agents. Virtually all initial orders from the second-moving side were placed exactly at the agent\'s reservation price, fully conceding rent (Figure \\\\ref{fig:first-mover}, left panel). The single exception occurred when the initial offer was immediately crossed by the opposing side and resulted in a trade. Interestingly, in GPT Small this pattern is partly reversed: in some runs the first-moving side posts at its reservation price while the second-moving side attempts to extract rent (Figure \\\\ref{fig:first-mover}, right panel).\\n\\n\\n\\\\section{Analysis of Reasoning of LLM Traders}\\n\\\\label{sec:reasoning}\\nSection~\\\\ref{sec:individual} identified willingness to cross the spread as the\\nbehavioral lever separating functioning markets from stalled ones. We exploit the\\ninternal thinking tokens of Gemini Large, which is the only model in our study that exposes reasoning traces, to ask what distinguishes the decision to keep\\nmaking incremental quote improvements from the decision to cross the spread and transact. Since only one model exposes its traces, we do not claim the pattern generalizes; we treat it as a window into a single mechanism we have already shown matters for efficiency, not as a claim about LLM traders in general.\\n\\nGemini Large agents alternate between minimal steps (the \\\\emph{incrementing\\nphase}) and larger jumps that cross the spread to secure a trade (the \\\\emph{cross\\nphase}). We show how a typical experiment unfolds in the supplementary material. To characterize how the reasoning differs between the two phases, we pool the\\ntraces from each phase and rank terms by the weighted log-odds-ratio with an\\ninformative Dirichlet prior \\\\citep{monroe2008fightin}, which measures how much\\nmore characteristic a term is of crossing than of incrementing. We group the most\\ndistinctive terms into four categories: \\\\textbf{Urgency} (\\\\textit{immediate,\\nwaiting, overthink}) and \\\\textbf{Execution \\\\& Certainty} (\\\\textit{secure,\\nguarantee, execute, lock}), associated with closing a trade; and \\\\textbf{Strategy\\n\\\\& Boundaries} (\\\\textit{strategic, position, room, competitive}) and\\n\\\\textbf{Optimization} (\\\\textit{improve, maximize, increment, increase}),\\nassociated with the margin-protecting reasoning of the incrementing phase. Moving\\nfrom the incrementing to the crossing phase, the first two categories rise sharply\\nwhile the latter two fall (Figure~\\\\ref{fig:cluster-shift}).\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure}[t]\\n    \\\\includegraphics[width=\\\\columnwidth]{Figures/lexical_shift.png}\\n    \\\\caption{Lexical shift in the internal thinking between move types, based on\\n    terms distinctively associated with urgency, execution, optimization, or\\n    strategy.}\\n    \\\\label{fig:cluster-shift}\\n\\\\end{figure}\\n\\nThis shift is consistent with the profit-versus-completion tradeoff of\\nSection~\\\\ref{sec:individual}. The language of margin protection recedes and the\\nlanguage of urgency and execution rises as agents move to trade. We read this as\\nagents weighting profit early and completion later. We are deliberately cautious\\nabout a stronger interpretation. A has value (3.25) and B has (2.25) in one assignment; the values are swapped in another. The same public actions are feasible in both, and the best attainable surplus is unchanged, yet this trade creates (2.50) surplus in the first assignment and (1.50) in the second. Q\'s experimenter can compute welfare because it knows the private values. The example limits a diagnostic based only on the public tape; it does not challenge Q\'s reported efficiency calculation.\\n\\n\\\\section{Objections and limits}\\n\\nP\'s ranking result needs reports from observers of the same underlying comparison, with errors that are independent once that comparison is fixed. Q records traders\' strategic actions under a shared order history, not those reports. The peers illustrated the problem with a hypothetical public anchor that every observer repeats regardless of the true comparison: perfect agreement would then convey no truth. This is an objection to applying P\'s assumptions to the auction tape, not an empirical finding that P\'s method fails on Q\'s data.\\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}', The thread looked for a way to connect P\'s methods to the trades that Q\'s agents often fail to complete. It found a payoff-equivalent completion signal and two limits on using P\'s ranking method with Q\'s public auction records. The payoff calculation is established prior work, and no one tested whether the signal changes trading or welfare, so the thread ended at PAUSE.\\n\\\\end{abstract}\\n\\n\\\\section{Introduction}\\n\\nQ, \\\\emph{Competitive Market Behavior of LLMs}, puts 11 language-model buyers and 11 sellers in a double\\nauction for five rounds \\\\cite{Q}. Each trader knows its own reservation price and sees the standing\\noffers and order history. A buyer can accept a standing ask by bidding at least that much; a seller can\\naccept a standing bid in the corresponding way. The agents are told to maximise their trading profit. Q\\nreports incomplete convergence, especially for GPT Large, whose agents often improve offers by small\\namounts until time runs out. Its analysis of Gemini Large reasoning traces links crossing a spread with\\nwords about urgency and execution, but does not establish what causes a trader to cross.\\n\\nP, \\\\emph{From Truthful Peer Signals to Contribution Rankings}, asks when noisy reports from several\\nobservers can be turned into a common ranking \\\\cite{P}. Its result needs repeated reports about the same\\nunderlying comparison, independent observer errors under stated conditions, and enough overlap between\\nobservers. It also discusses potential-based reward shaping: intermediate feedback can change while the\\ntotal reward difference between complete paths stays fixed. P\'s own labels ``Q\'\' and ``P\'\' refer to other\\npapers on mechanism design and cooperative credit, rather than to the assigned auction paper and P\\nitself.\\n\\nThe thread first asked whether P\'s peer calibration could diagnose Q\'s market. That route lacked the\\nreports P requires. The peers then pursued a narrower question: could a temporary signal for completing a\\ntrade change the behaviour of Q\'s fixed language-model traders while leaving final monetary profit\\nunchanged?\\n\\n\\\\section{What was done}\\n\\nThe peers checked the identity of the assigned papers before trying to combine their claims. They\\ncompared P\'s requirement for repeated, conditionally independent labels of one realised comparison with\\nQ\'s strategic bids, asks and shared public history. They found no direct input to P\'s calibration method\\nin the auction record. They also constructed two private-value assignments that give the same public\\ntrades but different realised welfare.\\n\\nThey next took P\'s reward-shaping calculation and adapted it to Q\'s undiscounted trading profit. They\\nproposed provisional feedback when a trader completes a trade, followed by a full reversal at settlement.\\nThey checked the resulting payoff path by path and compared the proposed claim with prior work on\\nmulti-agent reward shaping \\\\cite{devlin2011,lu2011}. Their source search also found a related LLM-guided\\ndouble-auction shaping study \\\\cite{related2025}; it did not establish novelty for this proposed\\nintervention.\\n\\nFinally, they tightened the proposed test after two objections. Q\'s prompts do not explicitly tell agents\\nthe numerical order cap or identify a final turn. Also, actions in an earlier round can affect later\\npublic histories. The peers therefore specified a disclosed final opportunity in the fifth round for a\\nlocal decision test, and separate paired full-market runs for a welfare test. They checked that Q\'s\\nwelfare measure is realised surplus, which need not move with trade count or price dispersion.\\n\\n\\\\section{Results}\\n\\nThe payoff calculation is exact for a completed round. Let \\\\(i\\\\) denote a trader, \\\\(t\\\\) a step in the\\nround, and \\\\(T\\\\) its settlement step. Let \\\\(U_i\\\\) be the trader\'s total profit without added feedback.\\nChoose a feedback balance \\\\(\\\\psi_{i,t}\\\\) that starts and ends at zero on every possible path. Give the\\ntrader the change \\\\(F_{i,t}=\\\\psi_{i,t+1}-\\\\psi_{i,t}\\\\) at each step. Then \\\\[ \\\\widetilde U_i\\n=U_i+\\\\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}F_{i,t} =U_i+\\\\psi_{i,T}-\\\\psi_{i,0} =U_i. \\\\] Here \\\\(\\\\widetilde U_i\\\\) is final profit\\nincluding the feedback. A temporary balance can rise when a trade is completed and return to zero at\\nsettlement. Because every complete path has the same final profit as before, profit best responses and\\nNash equilibria stay the same. This is P\'s telescoping argument in Q\'s setting, not a new equilibrium\\nresult \\\\cite{P,devlin2011,lu2011}. A change in fixed agents\' choices under the displayed feedback would\\nbe a behavioural finding about the feedback, not a change in the game\'s monetary incentives.\\n\\nThe peers\' welfare check also holds for Q\'s stated values. The five buyer--seller pairs with strictly\\npositive gains can produce surplus \\\\(2.50+2.00+1.50+1.00+0.50=7.50\\\\), the full available surplus. The\\nsixth pair has value and cost \\\\(2.00\\\\), so it adds no surplus. Thus five trades can achieve full\\nallocative efficiency even if their prices differ. A test of market improvement must measure realised\\nsurplus; crossing rates, trade count and price dispersion can help explain it but do not determine it\\n\\\\cite{Q}.\\n\\nThe public record alone cannot always reveal that surplus. In the peers\' example, a seller with cost\\n\\\\(0.75\\\\) trades with buyer A at price \\\\(2.00\\\\), while buyer B does not trade. A has value \\\\(3.25\\\\) and B\\nhas \\\\(2.25\\\\) in one assignment; the values are swapped in another. The same public actions are feasible\\nin both, and the best attainable surplus is unchanged, yet this trade creates \\\\(2.50\\\\) surplus in the\\nfirst assignment and \\\\(1.50\\\\) in the second. Q\'s experimenter can compute welfare because it knows the\\nprivate values.
